title: 🚦 Your API’s 429 Means You’ve Spent Your Tokens
ig_caption:
Stop blaming “random errors” — 429 is your rate limit talking. 
Here’s exactly what’s happening under the hood.

• Your API allows requests only when you have permission “tokens”
• Think: a bucket filled with tokens at a steady refill rate
• Each request costs tokens (spend permission slowly)
• If TOKENS LEFT hits 0, the API can’t grant access
• Result: DENIED → 429, so SERVED stays at 0
• In production: clients (📱) call the API, which may also coordinate with DB (💻) decisions

Practical takeaway: In interviews, describe rate limiting as a budget with refill over time (not just “block after N”). In production, return a clear Retry-After and implement client-side backoff.

What would you choose: strict token bucket (smooth throttling) or leaky bucket (constant outflow)—and why?
fb_caption:
A 429 response is not a vague failure—it’s explicit policy: “your client exceeded the allowed request budget.” In most systems, this is implemented with a rate-limiting algorithm that tracks permission over time.

What the visual shows (token bucket model)
- Tokens represent permission to perform work.
- A bucket refills tokens gradually (refill over time), which models the system’s capacity.
- Each incoming request consumes tokens.
- When TOKENS LEFT reaches 0, the API cannot serve; it returns DENIED with HTTP 429 and (effectively) SERVED is 0.

Why this matters architecturally
- Protects shared resources: Without limits, bursts can overwhelm CPU, DB connections, caches, or upstream dependencies.
- Separates “capacity management” from “business logic”: Rate limiting should fail fast before expensive work.
- Creates fairness: Limits per client/key (e.g., user, API key, IP, tenant) reduce noisy-neighbor effects.

Trade-offs and production lessons
- Token bucket vs. fixed window:
  - Token bucket smooths bursts while enforcing an average rate.
  - Fixed windows can cause edge-of-window spikes and uneven user experience.
- Client behavior:
  - Rate limits only work if clients respect them.
  - Use exponential backoff with jitter when receiving 429.
  - Prefer honoring Retry-After when provided.
- Correctness under concurrency:
  - Token accounting must be atomic and consistent across instances.
  - Common patterns: centralized store (e.g., Redis with atomic Lua), or per-instance limits with downstream global protection.
- Observability:
  - Track 429 rate, per-key top offenders, and “near-miss” metrics (tokens low) to tune refill rates.

Practical engineering recommendation
- Implement token bucket rate limiting with Retry-After, and add client-side backoff so you recover gracefully instead of creating retry storms.

Debate question: Should you rate limit by IP, API key, or user identity—and what failure mode worries you most (NAT sharing, key leakage, or account-level abuse)?
threads_caption: 429 isn’t random—it’s a token bucket saying “no more permission right now.” Tokens refill over time; when they hit 0 you get denied. Which rate-limit key would you pick: ip, api key, or user?
